chapter_theme: Hostility, as a disease of the disposition to quarrel. Giving it up is shown as gain and strength more than as saintliness, and pursuing it as a way to one's own ruin.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar: its defect (851), the good of not quarrelling (852-855), the harm of quarrelling (856-857), and both together (858-860).

851.reading: They call hostility the disease that spreads, among all living beings, the ill nature of division.
851.nuance: Hostility here is not an event but a disease that spreads a disposition. Parimelazhagar sees in எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் a judgement: quarrelling humans are being put with the animals.

852.reading: Even if someone does what you can't bear, intending division, it is best not to do harm in return, intending hostility.
852.nuance: The reason Parimelazhagar gives is strategic rather than saintly. Retaliate and enmity grows and you sink, abstain and it dies down and you rise. This is non-retaliation argued in the Book of Wealth's terms.

853.reading: If the painful disease called hostility is removed, it gives a light that doesn't diminish and has no flaw.
853.nuance: Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar differ on விளக்கம்: fame for one, radiance for the other. His route to fame is a long chain. Everyone becomes a friend, then every wealth comes, then giving, then renown. The verse takes no such steps.

854.reading: If the suffering of sufferings called hostility is destroyed, it brings the joy of joys.

positions.position: The joy is worldly: with everyone a friend, one obtains every fruit.
The joy is liberation, the highest of all joys.
positions.quote: எல்லா இன்பத்தின் மிக்க வீடுபேற்றின்பம் எய்தும் என்றவாறு.

855.reading: Who would set out to defeat those who are able to lean away from hostility?
855.nuance: வல்லாரை marks it as an ability, not a weakness. Manakkudavar faces the objection directly: wouldn't giving way be a defeat? The verse answers that no one can defeat them. Parimelazhagar adds it is particularly hard for kings.

856.reading: The life of one who says it is sweet to excel in hostility is close to failure and to ruin.
856.nuance: The problem is the relish: என்பவன் indicts the person who enjoys conflict and not one drawn into it. Kalaignar gives 'easy' (எளிது) for the verse's 'sweet' (இனிது), which changes the charge from pleasure to overconfidence.

857.reading: Those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the true thing that holds victory.
857.nuance: Parimelazhagar's point: hostility itself clouds the mind, so that the very quarrel blinds one to how to win. A combative person is therefore bad at conflict.

positions.position: மெய்ப்பொருள் here is the content of the treatises on policy, which brings success to those who follow them.
It is truth as such, which those in conflict can't perceive.

858.reading: Leaning away from hostility is gain; if one drives on to excel at it, ruin drives on to come.
858.nuance: Ruin mirrors what one does: ஊக்கின் ஊக்கும். Parimelazhagar locates the turning point in one's own mind, at the moment when hostility arises and isn't taken up.

859.reading: When gain is coming one doesn't look at hostility, and to bring on ruin one looks to excel at it.
859.nuance: This complicates 858. Hostility may not be the cause of ruin but the sign of it. Parimelazhagar says these are forerunners of gain and loss, and Manakkudavar links them to one's merit, which reduces how much the choice in 858 is really free.

860.reading: From hostility come all ills, and from friendly gladness comes the pride of good and fitting ways.
860.nuance: செருக்கு is usually a fault in the Kural (844) and here it is praise. Parimelazhagar reads it as great wealth, and நன்னயம் as good policy. So the virtue is presented as a prosperous kind of wisdom.

links.note: Both tell the injured not to return harm, but their reasons differ. In 314 the wrongdoer is shamed by kindness. In 852, on Parimelazhagar's reading, one's own position is improved. The same act is justified in moral terms in one book and in terms of advantage in another.

829 tells one to answer hidden contempt with hidden death. 852 says not to return harm even to one who plans division. They are three chapters apart in the same stretch on friends and foes, and the Kural offers both as sound counsel.

Two kinds of invincibility, each put as 'don't attempt it'. 771's warrior warns that those who stood before his lord now stand as stones. 855's person is unbeatable because he leans away. One's strength is in striking and the other's in declining.

784 says friendship isn't for laughter (நகுதல்). 860 makes நகல் the very source of good ways, which Parimelazhagar glosses as friendship. The same root gets very different valuations in the chapter on what friendship is for and the chapter on hostility.

source_issues: 856: Manakkudavar's text is cut off at the end (உண்டாமென்).
